# University of Edinburgh Summary
The University of Edinburgh traces its origins to a 1557 bequest from Bishop Robert Reid of St Magnus Cathedral, which envisioned the teaching of rhetoric and poetry alongside traditional subjects. After delays due to the Reformation Parliament of 1560, a royal charter was granted on April 14, 1582, empowering the town council to establish the college of higher education. Initially named Tounis College, it opened in 1583, covering liberal arts and divinity, and was later renamed "Colledge of King James" before gradually becoming the University of Edinburgh in the 17th century.
During the 18th century, the university became a central figure in the Scottish Enlightenment due to its democratic and secular origins, flexible professorship model, and lack of land endowments. This era attracted key figures like Adam Smith, David Hume, and Joseph Black. The university established itself as a leading medical school in the English-speaking world during this time, contributing to the international reputation of its graduates. The Edinburgh Seven, the first matriculated female students at any British university, began studying medicine there in 1869, leading to national political change.
